opus-5.5.text:
For me, writing code keeps me honest. When you're running a company like Taichi Graphics, it's very easy to drift into a world of slides, meetings, and abstract strategy, and slowly lose touch with what's actually hard about the product. If I'm still in the codebase, I know where the real bottlenecks are, I know which promises are realistic, and I can tell when an estimate is too optimistic or too conservative. That makes my decisions much better.

There's also a cultural reason. Our team is mostly engineers, and engineers respect people who build. If I can sit down, read a pull request carefully, and contribute something meaningful, it shows that I'm not just setting goals from far away. I'm in the trenches with them, and I understand the trade-offs they face every day. That trust is really valuable, especially at a startup.

And honestly, I just enjoy it. I started Taichi because I loved building tools for computer graphics and simulation. Writing code is how I think. Sometimes the best way for me to figure out a product direction is to prototype it myself over a weekend and see how it feels. Of course, as the company grows, I can't be writing the core of everything, and I shouldn't be a bottleneck. So the balance shifts toward hiring great people and getting out of their way. But I think keeping at least one hand on the keyboard is important. Once you completely stop, you start losing the intuition that made you good at this in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says that leaving the codebase can make a CEO lose touch with what is hard, misjudge bottlenecks, and make overly optimistic estimates, communicating the risk of underestimating engineering complexity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I never really stopped being an engineer, and I don't want to.

When I started Taichi as a PhD student, the whole point was to build a language that made it easier for people to write high-performance code for graphics and simulation. If I stopped writing code myself, I'd lose touch with the exact thing I'm supposed to be making decisions about. It's very easy for a CEO to sit in meetings all day and hear about the product secondhand. But hearing "the compile time is a little slow" from someone else is a completely different experience from sitting there yourself, waiting thirty seconds for a kernel to compile, and feeling that frustration. That feeling is what tells you what actually matters.

The second reason is that in a developer tools company, your users are engineers, and they can smell it when the leadership doesn't understand their pain. If I'm reviewing pull requests, filing issues, and shipping small features, I can talk to our community as a peer. That credibility is hard to earn any other way.

And third, frankly, it keeps me grounded about what's realistic. When you don't code, you start to believe every feature is a two-week project. When you do code, you remember that the last 10 percent of a feature takes as long as the first 90. That makes me a better planner and, I hope, a more reasonable boss.

I will say the balance shifts over time. I write much less code than I did three years ago, and I try not to be on the critical path for anything, because the team shouldn't be blocked waiting on the CEO. But I still want to be close enough to the codebase that I can read a diff and understand what's going on. The day I can't do that, I think I'd be running a very different company than the one I set out to build.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that without coding, a CEO may assume every feature is a two-week project, while coding reveals the work’s complexity and effort.

astra-6.text:
I think writing code keeps me connected to the reality of what we’re building. As a CEO, you spend a lot of time in meetings, and it’s easy to develop an understanding of the product that’s a little too abstract. When you actually implement something, you run into the details—the things that are harder than they sound, or the opportunities that aren’t obvious in a presentation.

It also helps me communicate with the engineering team. I can better understand the tradeoffs they’re making and ask more useful questions. Of course, I have to balance that with my responsibilities as CEO. I shouldn’t become a bottleneck or try to make every technical decision. But staying hands-on helps me keep my judgment grounded.

r001.rationale: The response says that without hands-on coding, a CEO’s understanding can become too abstract, while implementing features reveals details that are harder than they sound. This conveys the risk of underestimating engineering complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think writing code keeps me connected to what we’re actually building. As a CEO, you spend a lot of time in meetings, and it’s easy to develop an understanding of the product that’s a little too abstract. When you implement something yourself, you run into the details—the limitations of the tools, the complexity of the system, the things that sound easy but are actually hard.

That also helps me communicate with the engineering team. I can understand the tradeoffs better and ask more useful questions. Of course, I shouldn’t become a bottleneck or try to review every technical decision. But staying hands-on helps me keep my judgment grounded. And I enjoy it. Building something and seeing it work is still very satisfying.

r001.rationale: The candidate says hands-on implementation exposes the system’s complexity and reveals that tasks that sound easy can actually be hard, indicating that CEOs who don’t code may underestimate engineering problems.
